newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan opposition blasts LDP 'revenge budget' plan.
newsitem.headline: Japan opposition blasts LDP 'revenge budget' plan.

text.p: Japanese opposition leaders grilled Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday over calls within the ruling party to draft a "revenge budget" with reduced spending on districts which voted against the LDP in October polls.
"Is the LDP using taxpayers' money as a political tool?" Yukio Hatoyama, leader of the Democratic Party, asked Hashimoto in parliamentary debate.

Takeo Nishioka, whose New Frontier Party (NFP) was the main target of the "revenge budget" scheme floated by some LDP lawmakers last week, called on Hashimoto to apologise for the threat to "destroy democracy".
"I strongly demand that you retract the outrageous line and apologise to the public," Nishioka, the NFP secretary-general, told Hashimoto during questioning at a Lower House plenary session.
Japanese media last week reported that some senior LDP officials suggested punishing districts which voted for the NFP by trimming funds dispersed to local government for public works.
Taku Yamasaki, policy affairs chairman of the LDP, said on a television talk show on Sunday that such suggestions were made but said they did not reflect official party policy.
Hashimoto, who is concurrently LDP president, told parliament that "the allocation and implementation of the state budget will be carried out strictly and fairly, in light of the aims of policy".
In general elections for the 500-seat Lower House on October 20, the LDP won 239 seats and its bitter rival the NFP received 156.
Hashimoto was re-elected prime minister on November 9, forming a loose alliance with the LDP's former coalition partners, the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake party.
The parliamentary debut of the LDP minority government was overshadowed by financial scandals involving officials of the health and trade ministries.

The widening scandals, which have highlighted close ties and suspected exchanges of favours between bureaucrats and the industries they supervise, forced Hashimoto to revise his parliamentary address to include an apology.
"I feel nothing but shame for a series of events that have caused public confidence in government administration to plummet," Hashimoto told parliament last week.
